title: Who Gets to Teach Your Son What a Man Is?
author: Anthony B. Bradley
summary: Anthony Bradley responds to a Lancet Viewpoint in which Sarah Hawkes and Kent Buse propose treating the manosphere as a public health problem. He summarizes their case that these online communities exploit boys who feel they do not belong, and their six recommended areas for action, including regulating platform incentives and promoting healthy masculinities. He then sets out Ella Whelan's UnHerd counterargument that the framing pathologizes a question of moral evaluation, treats boys as victims without agency, and wrongly leans on speech regulation. Bradley's own diagnosis is that the debate exposes how irrelevant Christianity has become as a perceived source of solutions to social problems. He argues that government is not an institution that shapes virtue and should not define manhood. His conclusion is that boys need formation in virtue and a framework for heroic masculinity, which public policy cannot supply.
points: The Lancet authors frame the manosphere as a commercial ecosystem that fills a belonging gap for boys, which leads them to recommend platform regulation alongside efforts to promote healthy masculinities.

Whelan's critique is that adults have lost the confidence to tell young men that certain ideas are stupid and harmful, and that treating boys as helpless victims feeds the victimhood narratives influencers profit from.
Bradley reads the dispute as evidence that the church is no longer treated as a real answer to the formation of boys, with 'take the boys to church' not even an afterthought.
He objects that government has no standing to define what a man is, since it is not an institution that shapes virtue.
The positive claim is that boys need a framework for heroic masculinity grounded in virtue and transcendent moral excellence, not threats of punishment.
quotes: The idea that government should provide society with the best definition of what it means to be a man is unbelievably outrageous. Government is not an institution that shapes virtue.
The business models of these platforms incentivize inflammatory misogynistic content and performances of offended masculinity; anger and grievance drives engagement and profit.

First, defining misogynistic online content as a public health issue pathologizes what is essentially a question of moral evaluation and cultural authority. Toxic ideas directed at young people are not new.

Boys can think for themselves, assess arguments, and reject bad ideas. Presenting young men as powerless to resist viral headlines and algorithms only makes them more vulnerable to the kinds of victimhood narratives that Andrew Tate and others make money from.
Take the boys to church,” is no longer a solution. It’s not even an afterthought.
Ironically, there is no simultaneous call to regulate terrible content aimed at girls.
If you want boys to avoid manosphere content, they need to be formed with the types of virtues, goals, and aspirations that point them towards transcendent moral excellence.
What boys need is a framework for heroic masculinity, and public policy officials will not be able to provide that.
